issues.legal_issue: The government may alter a planning authority’s proposed development-plan modification when deciding whether to sanction it, provided the modification does not change the plan’s basic character.
material_facts: The planning authority published proposed changes, invited objections and suggestions, and submitted the proposed modification to the government for sanction.
The government sanctioned the proposal with an addition that had not appeared in the planning authority’s submission.
The challenge asserted that the government lacked power to make that addition.
issues.conclusion: The government had power to sanction the modification with changes and conditions, or to refuse sanction, and the contrary view of the High Court could not be sustained.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 37(1) and 37(2) of the Maharashtra Regional and Town Planning Act, 1966, the planning authority’s proposal must not change the basic character of the development plan; after the statutory consultation process, the government may sanction a modification with or without changes, impose conditions, or refuse sanction. The government has wide discretion in this legislative function, subject to review for arbitrariness or unreasonableness.

rule.if: statutory_planning_rule_challenge and planning_authority_submitted_consulted_modification and modification_preserved_plan_character and government_considered_sanction

predicates.statutory_planning_rule_challenge: A party challenged a rule governing development planning made through a statutory planning process.
predicates.planning_authority_submitted_consulted_m: The planning authority invited public objections and suggestions and then submitted its proposed modification to the government.
predicates.modification_preserved_plan_character: The proposed modification did not change the basic character of the development plan.
predicates.government_considered_sanction: The government considered whether to approve the submitted modification.
predicates.government_may_sanction_with_changes_or_: The government may approve the modification with changes or conditions.

issues.definition: When a planning authority submits a consulted modification that preserves the plan’s basic character for government sanction, the government may approve it with changes or conditions.

issues.legal_issue: A public hearing is not required before final government sanction of delegated planning legislation when the governing enactment does not provide for one.
material_facts: The planning authority invited objections and suggestions and gave affected persons an opportunity to be heard before submitting the proposed modification.
The enactment provided for government inquiry as the government considered necessary but did not prescribe a hearing before final sanction.
The challenge asserted that affected persons had to be heard again before the government sanctioned the modification.
issues.conclusion: The enactment did not require a hearing before final sanction, and natural justice could not be read into this legislative process to create such a requirement.
issues.legal_principle: Delegated legislation is not invalid for failure to comply with natural justice in its making unless the statute requires notice or a hearing. An enabling provision allowing the subordinate legislative body to make such inquiry as it considers necessary facilitates obtaining information and does not itself create a hearing right. The Court relied on Union of India v. Cynamide India Ltd., HSSK Niyami v. Union of India, and Canara Bank v. Debasis Das.

predicates.delegated_rulemaking_challenge: A party challenged the making of delegated legislation.
predicates.enactment_silent_on_hearing_at_final_san: The governing enactment did not require notice or a hearing before the final sanction of the delegated legislation.
predicates.hearing_not_required_at_final_sanction: A hearing is not required before final sanction.

issues.definition: When delegated legislation is challenged and the governing enactment does not require a hearing before final sanction, a hearing is not required at that stage.

issues.legal_issue: A court should not interfere with delegated legislative action when arbitrariness or unreasonableness has not been shown.
material_facts: The respondents challenged the government’s addition on the ground that the government lacked authority to make it.
The respondents did not contend that the challenged change was arbitrary or unreasonable.
issues.conclusion: The challenge did not justify judicial interference on grounds of arbitrariness or unreasonableness.
issues.legal_principle: Making or amending development control rules is a legislative function. Courts do not interfere with such action unless arbitrariness or unreasonableness is shown; the Court referred to ONGC v. Association of Natural Gas Consuming Industries of Gujarat.

predicates.delegated_legislation_challenge: A party challenged action taken in making delegated legislation.
predicates.no_arbitrariness_or_unreasonableness_sho: The party challenging the delegated legislation did not show that the action was arbitrary or unreasonable.
predicates.court_should_not_interfere: A court should not interfere with the delegated legislative action.

issues.definition: When delegated legislation is challenged but arbitrariness or unreasonableness is not shown, a court should not interfere.

issues.legal_issue: Promissory estoppel cannot be used to prevent the application of a statutory rule.
material_facts: The respondents relied on promissory estoppel to argue that the corporation should not insist on applying the additional floor-space-index requirement to the same plot.
The development control rules were made under statutory authority and had statutory force.
issues.conclusion: The High Court erred in applying promissory estoppel to prevent the corporation from relying on the statutory rule.
issues.legal_principle: Rules made under statutory authority form part of the statute, and promissory estoppel cannot operate against a statute. The Court relied on General Officer Commanding-in-Chief v. Subhash Chandra Yadav, A.P. Pollution Control Board II v. M.V. Nayudu, Sales Tax Officer v. Shree Durga Oil Mills, and Sharma Transport v. Government of Andhra Pradesh.

predicates.promissory_estoppel_claim_against_statut: A party invoked promissory estoppel to resist the application of a rule having statutory force.
predicates.rule_made_under_statutory_authority: The rule was made under authority conferred by statute.
predicates.promissory_estoppel_cannot_override_stat: Promissory estoppel cannot prevent the application of the statutory rule.

issues.definition: When a party invokes promissory estoppel against a rule made under statutory authority, the estoppel cannot override that rule.
